title: Slaughter birds in a poultry abattoir

lessons.title: Humane slaughter and the law
lessons.html:
Responsibility at the kill point

Slaughter is the point where a live bird becomes food. It must be done humanely, hygienically and efficiently. South African abattoirs work under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and its regulations, and cruelty to animals is an offence under the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962. Many plants also meet retailer welfare standards and, where applicable, religious requirements such as halal, under supervision of the certifying body.

Principles of humane slaughter

  • Birds must be handled calmly and hung correctly by both legs.
  • Birds must be rendered unconscious by stunning before the neck cut, unless the plant operates an approved religious slaughter method under its own procedure.
  • The neck cut must follow stunning quickly, before the bird can recover.
  • The bird must be dead from bleeding before it enters the scalder.

Why it matters for quality

Poor stunning and slaughter cause wing flapping, broken bones, bruising, red wing tips and poorly bled carcasses with red skin. Poorly bled carcasses are downgraded or condemned by inspection. Good practice therefore protects both welfare and profit.

Your responsibility at NQF level 3

You may operate or supervise the stunner and kill line. You must be trained and authorised, know the plant's settings and standards, check that each bird is properly stunned and killed, and stop the line or call the supervisor if something goes wrong.

Example

An operator notices that several birds are flapping after the stunner. He tells the supervisor at once. The water level in the stunner had dropped, so heads were not making contact. The level is corrected and the birds are checked again.

lessons.title: Stunning and killing
lessons.html:
The process step by step

Stunning

The most common method in South African poultry plants is the electrical water bath stunner: the bird's head is drawn through electrified water while the shackle line completes the circuit. Some plants use controlled atmosphere stunning with gas mixtures before hanging. Settings such as current, frequency and time are set by the plant according to its approved procedure and the type and size of bird.

Checking stunning effectiveness

Watch birds as they leave the stunner. Signs of an effective stun include: neck arched, wings held close, no rhythmic breathing, no eye blinking when the eye is touched, and no attempt to raise the head. Signs of a poor stun include birds that flap, lift their heads, vocalise or blink. Report poor stunning at once so settings or water level can be corrected.

The neck cut

The cut is made by an automatic killing machine or by hand with a sharp knife. It must sever the main blood vessels in the neck (carotid arteries and jugular veins) so bleeding is rapid. A back-up operator with a knife stands after the machine to cut any bird the machine missed. No bird may enter the scalder alive.

Bleeding

Birds pass through a bleed tunnel for the time set by the plant. Blood is collected and handled as a by-product; it must not enter drains uncontrolled.

Knife safety

Keep knives sharp, use a mesh glove on the non-knife hand where required, cut away from your body, and sterilise knives in the steriliser between uses.

lessons.title: Monitoring, hygiene and problems
lessons.html:
Keeping the kill line safe and under control

Routine checks

CheckWhy
Stunner settings and water levelEnsures every bird is stunned effectively
Birds after stunnerDetects poor stuns quickly
Neck cut on each birdEnsures complete bleeding
Birds entering scalderNo live birds; red carcasses mean poor bleeding
Knife sharpness and steriliser temperatureClean, effective cuts
Line speedMust allow correct stunning and cutting

Recording

Record stunner settings, checks, the number of birds missed by the machine and any welfare incidents on the plant forms. Records show the inspector and auditors that welfare and hygiene are controlled.

Hygiene at the kill point

The kill area is a dirty area with blood and feathers. Keep blood in the collection trough, clean splashes regularly, and do not carry knives or equipment into clean areas. Wash hands and aprons often.

When things go wrong

  • Power failure or stunner fault: stop the line; birds on the line must be dealt with humanely as the plant emergency procedure says.
  • Many missed cuts: adjust or stop the killing machine; add back-up staff.
  • Line jam: stop the line using the emergency stop; never reach into moving machinery. Lock out before clearing.

Electrical safety

The stunner uses electricity and water. Only authorised people adjust it. Never touch the stunner water or electrodes while it is live.

Key points

  • Slaughter must be humane under the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 and hygienic under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000.
  • Birds must be stunned effectively and cut quickly before they can recover.
  • A back-up operator must cut any bird missed by the killing machine; no live bird may enter the scalder.
  • Check stun signs, record settings and report problems immediately.
  • Never touch a live stunner or reach into moving machinery.

quiz.question: What is the most common stunning method in South African poultry plants?
Which sign shows a bird has NOT been stunned effectively?

options.text: The bird lifts its head and blinks

quiz.question: Which blood vessels should the neck cut sever?

options.text: The carotid arteries and jugular veins

quiz.question: What is the job of the back-up operator after the killing machine?

options.text: To cut any bird the machine missed
